conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool today called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of ten questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. Nothing you share will leave this room unless you or your baby’s safety is at risk, so please feel free to speak openly; this is a judgment-free space. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about “right” or “wrong” answers. Ready to begin?

In the past seven days, how have you felt about moments of laughter or looking forward to enjoyable things—has that been easy to come by, or has it felt more distant?

Honestly, it’s been… kind of distant. I used to laugh at my favorite shows or get excited about little things—like a fancy coffee or a new episode of that podcast I like—but now it feels flat. When people try to joke with me, I’ll smile, but it doesn’t really land inside. I can’t remember the last time I truly looked forward to something just for me.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often… maybe once or twice this week I sort of chuckled, but it felt forced. Mostly I can’t find the energy to laugh, even when something’s genuinely funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Hardly at all. I catch myself thinking, “I should be excited about that,” but the feeling just isn’t there. Even planning a short walk or ordering food I used to love feels like another chore on the list.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot of the time. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m not good enough at this.” I’ll replay every little choice I made—did I eat something that upset her? Did I pick her up too fast?—and end up feeling like it’s all my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often—sometimes it feels like my heart’s racing and I can’t settle, even when everything’s calm. I’ll lie in bed running through all the ways something could go wrong with the baby: what if she stops breathing, what if I drop her, what if I miss some sign she’s sick? I know it’s not logical, but I can’t shut the thoughts off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—several times this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight, my breathing speeds up, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even though I can’t name what. It passes after a bit, but it leaves me shaky and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most of the time. It feels like every task—changing a diaper, folding laundry, even brushing my teeth—gets piled on top of the last one until I can’t see over the heap. I manage to push through, but by the end of the day I’m just spent and teary.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps circling through all the “what-ifs” and things I think I messed up. Some nights I’m still awake when the baby wakes for her next feed, and even when I do drift off, I jolt awake sure I heard her cry. It’s like I can’t trust myself to rest.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes, quite a lot. It’s like a heavy blanket that settles over me most days. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel weepy, or I’ll watch my partner sleeping and just feel this ache. I keep telling myself I should be happy—she’s healthy, we’re safe—but the sadness keeps leaking through anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… it happens a few times each week. Sometimes it’s because I’m just worn out, sometimes it’s triggered by something tiny, like spilling a bottle I just pumped. The tears come fast and hard, and once they start it’s hard to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening note – Postpartum visit

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, frequent crying (Q8, 9)  
- Marked anhedonia, loss of anticipatory pleasure (Q1, 2)  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Near-daily anxiety, panic spells with somatic arousal (Q4, 5)  
- Subjective overwhelm, sense of inability to cope (Q6)  
- Mood-congruent insomnia (initial, mid) (Q7)  

Pattern  
Consistent depressive and anxiety symptoms present most days for ≥2 weeks; no self-harm ideation reported (Q10).

Screening significance  
Findings exceed “baby blues” threshold; meet provisional criteria requiring further evaluation for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and co-occurring Anxiety Disorder.  
Risk factors: anhedonia, guilt, panic, functional compromise, sleep loss.

Next step  
Schedule follow-up assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7, Edinburgh) and discuss supports; safety plan reviewed—return sooner if any self-harm thoughts develop.
